questions.question: Define shear and torsion, give one everyday example of each, and describe how a member fails under each.
questions.expected_answer: Shear acts across a member when two forces push in opposite directions on either side of a plane through it, so one part tends to slide past the other; examples: scissors cutting paper, a bolt between two plates pulled in opposite directions, a nail in a joint. A member fails in shear by being sliced through across that plane. Torsion is twisting, when one end of a member is turned while the other is held or turned the opposite way; examples: wringing a cloth, a screwdriver shaft, a bakkie drive shaft, a crank axle. A member fails in torsion by twisting off, with its outer fibres failing along a spiral line.

questions.question: Explain where shear and torsion occur in real structures and which shapes of member resist each.
questions.expected_answer: Shear occurs in connections (bolts, rivets, nails, pins, nail plates) wherever joined parts try to slide past each other, in the ends of beams near their supports where the load transfers into the wall, and in buildings in earthquakes or floods where floors try to slide sideways; it is resisted by enough material across the plane of sliding, such as thick bolts used in pairs, deep beam webs and shear walls. Torsion occurs in every shaft transmitting rotary motion and wherever a load is applied off the centre line of a member, such as a one-sided sign or balcony; it is resisted by shapes with material far from the axis, especially hollow tubes, which beat solid rods of the same weight.

questions.question: Describe the arrow symbols for the four forces and identify the force on each of these carport members: the posts under the roof weight, the diagonal cable brace, the base bolts in a side wind, and the front beam with sheeting fixed on one side being lifted by wind.
questions.expected_answer: Tension: two arrows along the member pointing away from each other out through the ends. Compression: two arrows along the member pointing towards each other. Shear: two parallel arrows across the member, close together, pointing in opposite directions on either side of the sliding plane. Torsion: two curved arrows around the member at its ends turning in opposite directions. Posts: compression. Diagonal cable: tension. Base bolts in a side wind: shear. Front beam with one-sided lifting load: torsion.
